title: How to Open a TXT File: Which Program to Use on Any Device
desc: Which program opens a .txt file: Notepad on Windows, TextEdit on a Mac, Files on iPhone, Android apps or a browser, and how to fix text with strange characters.
h1s: How to open a TXT file: which program to use on any device
headings: How to open a TXT file: which program to use on any device
In your browser, without installing anything
When the text shows strange characters
Fix the encoding without uploading the file
text: HomeGuidesHow to open a TXT fileHow to open a TXT file: which program to use on any deviceThe program that opens a text file on Windows, Mac, iPhone and Android, how to read one in a browser, and how to fix text that shows strange characters.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerA .txt file is plain text, so any text editor opens it and you do not need to install anything. On Windows it opens in Notepad, on a Mac in TextEdit, on an iPhone or iPad in the Files app, and on Android in Google Docs, Google Drive or the text viewer of your file manager. Every web browser can show one too. If the text appears as strange symbols, the program has guessed the wrong encoding; the fix is further down.On WindowsDouble-click the file and it opens in Notepad, which comes with every version of Windows. If another program opens it instead, right-click the file, choose Open with, then Notepad, and choose to always use it if you want it as the default.Notepad shows the text exactly as it is, with no formatting. File, Save as lets you choose the encoding of the copy you save.Microsoft Word also opens .txt files, and asks which encoding to use when it is not sure.Free code editors such as Notepad++ or Visual Studio Code handle large files and many encodings, and number the lines.On a MacDouble-click the file and it opens in TextEdit. To read it without opening any app, select it in Finder and press the Space bar for a quick preview. If TextEdit shows the wrong characters, open TextEdit, Settings (Preferences on older versions of macOS), Open and Save, set the plain text encoding for opening files to the right one, for example Unicode (UTF-8), and open the file again.On a phone or tabletOn an iPhone or iPad, tap the file in the Files app to read the text; to change it, share it to an app that edits text, such as Pages. On Android, tap the file in your file manager or downloads: most phones show plain text directly, or offer Google Docs or Google Drive to open it. A phone browser works as well: in the TXT editor here the tools fold into a sheet and the text fills the screen.In your browser, without installing anythingEvery browser displays a text file: drag it onto an open window, or press Ctrl+O (Cmd+O on a Mac) and choose it. That shows the text, but you cannot change it.To read and edit it, drop the file on the TXT editor. It opens with line numbers and search, and lets you type, find and replace, sort lines, remove duplicates and change case; Arabic lines show right to left. Download saves a copy in the encoding and line endings you choose. Your browser reads the file itself, so it is never uploaded, and the page keeps working offline once it has loaded.When the text shows strange charactersA text file stores only bytes. The encoding says which bytes stand for which letters, and the file does not say which one it uses, so every program guesses. When the guess is wrong, Arabic turns into strings like "Ø§Ù„" or question marks, and accented letters break. Three encodings cover almost every file you will meet:UTF-8 is the standard today and covers every language. Some programs put an invisible marker at the start of the file, the byte order mark or BOM, so that others recognise it.UTF-16 is written by some Windows programs and exports. A program that expects UTF-8 shows it with gaps between the letters, or as nonsense.Windows-1256 is the older Arabic encoding of Windows, still produced by some older systems. Programs that assume UTF-8 cannot read its Arabic letters.Fix the encoding without uploading the fileDrop the file on the TXT editor. It recognises UTF-8 with or without a BOM, UTF-16 and Windows-1256, and shows the encoding it found. If the text still looks wrong, choose another one in the Encoding group and click Reopen with this encoding.To pass the file on safely, download it as UTF-8, which every modern program reads; choose UTF-8 with BOM if it will be opened in older Windows programs that otherwise guess the old code page.Very large text filesLog files and data exports can run to hundreds of megabytes. Simple editors load the whole file at once and can become slow or stop responding with very large ones.The TXT editor has been tested with a 46 MB file, whose first lines appear in under half a second. Files over 50 MB show a warning first, and a file of more than about 2 million characters opens in a fast read view that draws only the lines on screen, while search and the other tools still work on the whole text. Beyond that, the limit is your device's memory. If the file is really a table of values separated by commas, the large CSV viewer is the better fit.What a .txt file isA .txt file holds only characters: letters, digits, spaces and line breaks. There is no bold, no font, no pictures and no page layout, which is why every device can open it and why it is used for notes, logs, lists and passing data between programs. Each line ends with an invisible line break: Windows writes CRLF, while Mac and Linux write LF. Most editors read both, and the TXT editor can save either. Files with other extensions, such as .log or .md, are plain text too and open in any text editor in the same way.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe what you see when you open the file (no personal data).

Excel and OpenAnyDoc both open it.What may look differentOnly Excel draws everything. When OpenAnyDoc saves a workbook it keeps values, formulas, number formats, merged cells and column widths, but not charts, images, pivot tables or conditional formats. title: How to Password Protect a PDF for Free, Without Uploading It
desc: Password-protect a PDF for free: the password to open versus print and copy restrictions, what a password stops, how to send it, and how to remove it later.
headings: What a password stops, and what it does not
Restrictions: when they are worth it
Removing or changing the password later
text: HomeGuidesPassword-protect a PDFHow to password-protect a PDFThe two kinds of PDF password, what each one really protects, and how to share a locked file safely.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerChoose the PDF in Protect PDF, type a password twice and download the locked copy. It is encrypted with AES-256 in your browser, and neither the file nor the password is uploaded; anyone who opens the copy needs the password. Send the password by a different route than the file, and keep the original, because a forgotten password cannot be recovered.Two kinds of PDF passwordA PDF can carry two different passwords, and they do very different jobs.The password to open encrypts the file. Without it, the pages cannot be read at all. This is the one that keeps a document private.A permissions password goes with restrictions on printing, copying text and pictures, or changing the document. The file opens without it, and the restrictions are a request that most PDF readers honour, not a lock. A PDF that opens freely but will not print has only restrictions, and Unlock PDF lifts them without any password, which shows how little they protect.Protect PDF always sets a password to open, of at least 4 characters. Untick Print, Copy text and pictures or Change the document if you also want restrictions, and add an optional permissions password.What a password stops, and what it does notA password to open keeps the content from anyone who has the file but not the password: an email sent to the wrong address, a lost USB stick, a shared folder with too many members. It does not stop everything:Anyone who has the password can read, print, photograph or forward the pages, and can save a copy without the password.The file name is not encrypted, so a name such as salary-review-2026.pdf already says what is inside. Give the file a plain name.A short or guessable password can be found by trying many passwords. AES-256 is the strongest encryption PDF readers support, but its strength depends on the password.A password does not show who sent the file or whether it was changed; that needs a certificate-based digital signature.Choose a password that holdsUse a long password: several unrelated words, with a number or a symbol between them, are easier to remember and harder to guess than one short word. Avoid names, dates of birth, phone numbers and anything printed in the document itself. Do not reuse a password from an email or bank account. Type it twice in Protect PDF; Show passwords lets you check it before you lock the file.Send the password separatelyA password in the same email as the file protects nothing: whoever gets the email gets both. Send the file one way and the password another:Email the PDF, then send the password in a text message or a chat app, or say it on a call.For someone you send files to often, agree a password once, in person or by phone, rather than sending a new one each time.Never put the password in the file name, the email subject or the document.Restrictions: when they are worth itRestrictions suit cases where you trust the reader but want to discourage casual changes, such as a final price list or a signed agreement sent for reference. Most readers will then grey out printing or copying. Do not rely on them for anything secret: anyone who can open the file can remove them, for example with Unlock PDF. If you set a permissions password, make it different from the password to open.Removing or changing the password laterYour original file stays on your device, unchanged and without a password, so keep it somewhere safe. To take the password off a locked copy, open it in Unlock PDF and type the password; it does not guess or crack passwords. To change a password, remove the old one there and protect the file again. Other tools, such as Merge PDF or Split PDF, need the password removed first.Other free waysOn a Mac, Preview can add a password when you export the PDF with File, then Export. Word and LibreOffice can encrypt a document with a password when they save it as a PDF, which suits a document you wrote yourself. Protect PDF works with any PDF that opens without a password, on any device, and keeps its text, pictures, links and form fields as they are.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe what you need to protect (no personal data, and never send a password).

title: PDF to ChatGPT Without Losing Tables: Paste It as Markdown
desc: Why tables break when you copy a PDF into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, how Markdown keeps rows and columns, and how to convert in your browser with no upload.
h1s: How to give ChatGPT a PDF without losing the tables
headings: How to give ChatGPT a PDF without losing the tables
Why tables fall apart when you copy a PDF
Why Markdown keeps rows and columns
Rows and columns you can check
How to do it, step by step
When the table still comes out wrong
For a large or messy table
text: HomeGuidesPDF tables in an AI chatHow to give ChatGPT a PDF without losing the tablesWhy copied PDF tables run together, how Markdown keeps every row and column, and what to check before you paste.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerTurn the PDF into Markdown first and paste that, not text copied straight from the PDF. A PDF stores words at positions on a page, not rows and columns, so a plain copy runs the cells of a table together; Markdown writes each row on its own line with a | between cells, which ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini read as a table. OpenAnyDoc's PDF to Markdown does this in your browser, and the file is never uploaded.Why tables fall apart when you copy a PDFA PDF is made for printing. Inside the file, a table is not a table: it is a set of short pieces of text, each placed at an exact spot on the page, plus some lines drawn around them. Nothing in the file says that "North" and "1,240" belong to the same row.When you select a table and copy it, your PDF reader guesses an order and joins the pieces with spaces or line breaks. A row like Region, Units, Total can arrive as three separate lines, or as one long line where you can no longer tell which number belongs to which column. An AI chat then has to guess the layout again, and a wrong guess shows up as a total in the wrong row or a summary that mixes two columns.Attaching the PDF to the chat does not remove the problem: the service reads the text out of the file in its own way, and you cannot see what it read before it answers. It also sends the whole file to that service, including pages you did not need to share.Why Markdown keeps rows and columnsMarkdown is plain text with a few marks for structure. A table is written row by row, with a | between cells and a line of dashes under the header, for example:| Region | Units | Total ||---|---|---|| North | 120 | 1,240 |Rows and columns you can checkEvery AI chat that reads Markdown understands this layout, and so can you: the cells are in plain sight, so you can check them before you send anything. text: HomeGuidesPDF tools without uploadPDF tools that do not upload your fileHow popular PDF sites handle your file, where they do more, and the tools that keep a PDF on your own device.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 17, 2026 · Updated November 23, 2026The short answerMost free online PDF tools, including iLovePDF, Smallpdf and the PDF24 website, upload your file to their servers, process it there and delete it after a set time. That is fine for many documents. If a file must not leave your device, use a tool that processes it locally: OpenAnyDoc in the browser, or a desktop app that works offline, such as PDF24 Creator on Windows. The facts below come from each service's own pages, checked on 17 November 2026.How popular PDF sites handle your file (checked 17 November 2026)What each service says on its own pages; follow the links for the current wording:iLovePDF: files are uploaded over HTTPS and kept "for a maximum of 2 hours" so you can download the result, then removed. A desktop app is available for Mac and Windows.Smallpdf: files are "permanently removed" from its servers one hour after processing. Smallpdf says it is ISO 27001 certified and stores files in the EU.PDF24 Tools (website): uploaded files are deleted from the processing server within one hour. PDF24 Creator, its Windows app, works offline and keeps all files on your computer.Sejda (website): its privacy policy says uploaded and output files are stored for processing and then permanently deleted, with no backups.Where those services do moreTo be fair about the choice: several of these sites give more settings for compressing a PDF (resolution and picture quality), convert to PDF/A, and have desktop apps, accounts with cloud storage and batch processing. If you need one of those and the document is not sensitive, they are reasonable choices.What OpenAnyDoc does differentlyEvery OpenAnyDoc PDF tool runs in your browser. The file is read, changed and saved on your device, and the page's security policy only lets it contact its own site, so there is no upload to delete later. You can check this yourself in the browser's network panel while a tool runs. title: Combine Photos Into One PDF: JPG, HEIC and PNG, No Upload
desc: Turn phone photos into one PDF: pick JPG, HEIC or PNG pictures, set their order, page size and margins, straighten document photos and keep the file small.
h1s: How to turn phone photos into one PDF
headings: How to turn phone photos into one PDF

text: HomeGuidesPhotos to one PDFHow to turn phone photos into one PDFOrder, page size and margins, photos of paper documents, and how to keep the PDF small enough to send.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026 · Updated November 23, 2026The short answerAdd the photos to JPG to PDF in your browser, drag them into order, choose a page size and margin, and download one PDF. It reads JPG, PNG and iPhone HEIC photos, as well as WebP, TIFF and other pictures, on your device, so nothing is uploaded. For photos of paper documents, Scan to PDF straightens each page first.Choose the photosOn a phone, open JPG to PDF and tap Choose a file: the phone offers its photo library as well as its files, so you can pick photos straight from the camera roll. On a computer, drop the pictures on the page. You can add more at any time.iPhones save photos as HEIC by default. Safari reads them itself; in Chrome, Edge and Firefox a HEIC decoder loads the first time you add one, and the photo is still read on your device. A few photos taken with the newest iPhone settings may not decode; save those as JPG on the phone first, or convert them with HEIC to JPG.Put them in orderThe order you pick photos in is not always the order the pages should have. Drag the pictures into place with a mouse, or use the buttons under each picture on a phone. The PDF follows this order, one picture per page. Photos that the phone saved sideways but marked as turned are drawn upright, so a portrait photo stays portrait.Page size, orientation and marginsThree settings decide how each photo sits on its page:Page size: A4 or Letter if the PDF will be printed or attached to a form (Letter is the usual paper size in the United States and Canada, A4 in most other countries), or Same as the picture if it will only be read on a screen.Orientation: Portrait, Landscape, or Follow each picture, which suits a mix of upright and wide photos.Margin: None, Small or Large. A small margin keeps a printer from cutting the edges; no margin suits a page the size of the picture.Photos of documents: use Scan to PDFA photo of a letter or a receipt taken at an angle looks crooked in a PDF, with a dark table around it. Scan to PDF fixes that: drag the four corners onto the paper's corners and the page is straightened as if it had been scanned flat, and its Document look turns the paper white and the ink dark, evening out shadows. You can take the photos from that page with the phone's camera.Either way, the pages are pictures, so the words cannot be searched or copied. To make them searchable, see how to make a scanned PDF searchable.Keeping the PDF smallJPG to PDF puts JPG and PNG photos into the PDF as they are, without compressing them again. Quality is kept, but the PDF is about as large as the photos together, and phone photos are often several megabytes each.To make it smaller, make the photos smaller first:Compress image: a quality of 75 usually gives files less than half the size, with a before and after view to check.Resize image: a photo for a document rarely needs the full camera resolution.Screenshots saved as PNG shrink less; convert them to JPG while compressing.Scan to PDF already reduces very large photos to 2,000 pixels on the long side of each page.Or make the finished PDF smaller with Compress PDF.Location and camera detailsPhone photos often record where and when they were taken and which phone took them. If the PDF is going to someone you do not know well, save clean copies of the photos first with Remove image metadata, which shows what each photo reveals before it removes it.One PDF, or one per photoIn JPG to PDF, click Make PDF, check the preview and download one PDF. If each photo should be its own file, tick One PDF per picture and you get a ZIP instead. To add the photos to a PDF you already have, make the photo PDF first and then join the two with Merge PDF; the guide on how to merge PDF files covers the order.On the phone itselfPhones have their own ways too. On an iPhone or iPad, the Files app can make one PDF from pictures you select (Create PDF, in the More menu), and the document scanner in the Files and Notes apps photographs pages straight into a PDF. On Android, the Google Drive app has a scanner that saves PDFs to your Drive. These give fewer choices of page size and margin, and Drive keeps the scan in your online account.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe the photos you are trying to combine (no personal data).

desc: Give a PowerPoint deck to ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini as a text outline with slide titles, bullet points and speaker notes, made in your browser with no upload.

headings: How to give a PowerPoint presentation to an AI chat

text: HomeGuidesPowerPoint to AI chatHow to give a PowerPoint presentation to an AI chatTurn a deck into an outline an AI chat can work through slide by slide, with the speaker notes, and know what the outline leaves out.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerTurn the deck into a text outline and paste that: one section per slide with its title, the slide's text as bullet points and the speaker notes underneath. OpenAnyDoc's PowerPoint to Markdown makes this outline from a .pptx file in your browser, without uploading it, so ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini can work slide by slide.Why a deck is hard to pasteThe words of a presentation are spread over dozens of separate text boxes. Copying them slide by slide is slow, since a forty-slide deck means forty rounds of copy and paste, and the order of the boxes often comes out wrong. The speaker notes, which usually hold the real explanation, sit in a separate pane and are easy to leave behind.Attaching the .pptx sends the whole file, pictures included, to the AI service, and you cannot see which text it picked up. A text outline is smaller, and you can read every word of it before you send it.What the outline looks likeEach slide follows the same pattern, numbered in the order of the slides in the file, so the chat can refer to "slide 4" and mean the same slide you do:# The deck's name, from the file name.## Slide 1: and the slide's title.- Each piece of text on the slide as a bullet point.> Speaker notes: written as a quote under their slide.How to do itPowerPoint to Markdown runs on your device, and nothing is sent to a server or to an AI service:Open PowerPoint to Markdown and choose a .pptx, .ppsx, .potx or .pptm file, or drop it on the page.The outline appears in a text box, with its token count.Read it through, then click Copy and paste it into the chat, or download the .md file.What the outline keeps and what it dropsThe outline carries the words of the file, read slide by slide. A few things are worth knowing:Titles come from the slide's title placeholder. A title typed into an ordinary text box shows up as a bullet point, and the slide is headed only Slide N.Indented sub-points come out at the same level as the points above them.Each cell of a table on a slide becomes its own bullet point.Hidden slides are included, so delete any you do not want to share.Pictures, charts, SmartArt and text inside pictures are left out.Comments left by reviewers are not included.Old .ppt files are not read; save them as .pptx in PowerPoint first.What to ask once it is pastedBecause every slide is labelled, you can ask for work slide by slide: a one-line summary of each slide, speaker notes for the slides that have none, a check that the notes and the slides say the same thing, or a shorter version of the deck for a ten-minute slot. Ask it to give the slide number with every change it suggests, so you can find each one quickly when you edit the deck. To see the slides as they were designed while you work, open the file in the PowerPoint viewer.Before you pasteSpeaker notes are written for the presenter, not the audience, so read them as well as the slides:Personal data: customer names, email addresses or phone numbers in notes or tables. Mask data replaces them on your device; it reads plain text files, so rename the downloaded .md file to .txt and open it there.Length: a long deck with full notes can use more tokens than you expect. The token count is shown with the outline; how many tokens a file uses explains the number.Documents tooFor a report written in Word, the same idea keeps its headings and lists: see giving a Word document to an AI chat.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe the presentation (no personal data).

title: Reduce Photo File Size for Email and Upload Limits
desc: Get a photo under 1 MB or any upload limit: resize first, pick the right quality and format, then check the result. Done in your browser, nothing uploaded.
h1s: How to reduce a photo's file size for email or a form
headings: How to reduce a photo's file size for email or a form
Why a phone photo is so large
Check the result before you send it
text: HomeGuidesReduce photo file sizeHow to reduce a photo's file size for email or a formResize, quality and format, in the order that saves the most, and how to check the file before a form refuses it.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerTo get a photo under a limit such as 1 MB, make it smaller in pixels first, then save it as a JPG at a lower quality. A phone photo resized to about 1600 pixels on its long side and saved at quality 75 usually ends up well under 1 MB. Compress image shows the new size as you move the quality slider, and the photo never leaves your device.Why a phone photo is so largeA photo from a recent phone holds millions of pixels, far more than a screen or an upload form needs, and every pixel takes space. The file is often several megabytes before you do anything to it. Two things decide its size: how many pixels it has, and how hard its format squeezes them. A size limit is easiest to meet by working on both, in that order.Many forms say what they accept, for example "JPG or PNG, under 1 MB", and sometimes a minimum width in pixels. Read that line first, because it decides the format and how far you can shrink the picture.Step 1: resize firstResizing removes pixels, and it saves more than any quality setting. Halving the width and the height leaves a quarter of the pixels, and the file shrinks with them. Open Resize image and choose one of three ways:Pixels: type a width such as 1600 and keep the aspect ratio on, so the photo is not stretched.Percent: shrink every picture by the same share, for example 50%.Ready sizes: Instagram and WhatsApp sizes, and common passport photo sizes at 300 dpi. These are common sizes, not official checks, so confirm the office's own rules.Resize image has the same format and quality fields as the compressor, so for a single photo one step can do both.Step 2: lower the qualityOpen Compress image, add the photo and move the quality slider. Quality 75 is a good start for photos: files are usually less than half the size and the difference is hard to see. The before-and-after view shows the first picture at that setting with its size before and after, so you can stop as soon as it is under the limit.There is no box where you type "under 1 MB": you choose the quality and read the size. If 75 is not enough, try a lower value and look at faces, small text and skies, where blocky patches show first. If the quality has to drop a long way to fit, go back and resize instead; a smaller sharp photo looks better than a large blurry one.Quality applies to JPG, WebP and AVIF. PNG is lossless: its pixels stay exactly the same, so a photo saved as PNG shrinks much less.Step 3: pick the formatThe format matters as much as the quality:JPG: accepted by every form, email app and phone. The safe choice when you are not sure.WebP: usually 25–35% smaller than JPG at the same look, and it keeps transparency. Image to WebP converts to it, but some older email apps, desktop programs and forms still refuse it, so check what the form accepts.PNG: right for screenshots, logos and pictures with flat colour or sharp text. Photos saved as PNG stay large; convert them to JPG or WebP.AVIF: often smaller still, but slow to save (a few seconds per large photo) and accepted by fewer forms.Check the result before you send itLook at the downloaded file, not only the number in the tool: the size in the preview is for the first picture, and each photo in a batch comes out a little different.Open it in the Image viewer to see its size in pixels, its file size and the picture zoomed in.Aim a little under the limit. text: HomeGuidesRemove location from a photoHow to remove the location from a photoWhat a photo file reveals, how to see it, and how to send a clean copy without uploading the original anywhere.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerIf location was on for the camera, a phone photo carries the exact GPS position where it was taken, along with the phone model and the date. To remove it, add the photo to Remove image metadata: it lists what the photo contains and saves a clean copy, in your browser and without uploading it. On an iPhone you can also leave the location out for one share, from the share sheet's Options.What a photo file carriesPhone cameras write details into each photo, beside the picture itself. This hidden part is called metadata, and most of it is stored as EXIF (some apps add XMP or IPTC fields too). It can include:GPS location: latitude and longitude, often precise enough to point at a single building, if location was allowed for the camera.The date and time the photo was taken.The phone or camera make and model, and the lens.The software that edited it, and sometimes an author name.Orientation: which way up the photo should be shown.Check what your photo revealsNone of this shows when you look at the photo, but anyone who gets the original file can read it. To see it yourself, open the photo in the Image viewer and open its details panel: it lists the camera, lens and date taken and, when the photo carries one, the GPS location, with a link to see it on OpenStreetMap if you choose to.Remove image metadata shows the same details for each photo in plain words, for example "This photo contains your GPS location", before you save anything.Remove it in your browserThe photo is read and cleaned on your device and never sent to a server; you can check that it is not uploaded with your browser's own tools.Open Remove image metadata and add one photo or many.Read what each photo lists: GPS location, camera, date and any other details found.Click Download clean copies. Several photos come as one ZIP.Will the photo lose quality?Not for JPG, PNG and WebP. Only the metadata is cut out and the picture data is copied as it is, so the photo looks exactly the same. A JPG keeps its colour profile, so colours don't shift. Each clean copy is read again before you get it, and the tool stops if any location, camera or date is still there.Two exceptions. HEIC and TIFF photos are saved again as a high-quality JPG. And a JPG with a sideways orientation tag is turned upright in its pixels first, because removing the tag would show it on its side, so its pixels change slightly.Stop the phone adding itPhone settings can leave the location out from the start, or for one share. Menu names change between versions and phone makers, so look for these words:iPhone, for one share: in the share sheet, tap Options at the top and turn off Location before you send.iPhone, for every new photo: Settings, Privacy & Security, Location Services, Camera, Never.Android: open the Camera app's settings and turn off the option for location tags or saving the location; its name depends on the phone maker.Don't social sites remove it anyway?Many sites remove location details when you post a photo, but not all of them do, and messaging apps differ: some drop it when they shrink a photo, while sending the same photo as a file or by email usually keeps everything. Settings and policies also change over time. Cleaning the photo yourself first means you don't need to know which is which.Photos you already took still carry their location even after you turn it off on the phone, so clean those before you send them.What removing metadata can't doA clean file can still give a place away through what is in the picture: a street sign, a house number, a number plate, a uniform or the view from a window. Faces are the same. Blur faces finds the faces and lets you drag over anything else, such as a badge or a number plate, before you share.File names are not changed, so rename a file named after a place or a person. And when you shrink a photo for email or convert it from HEIC to JPG, the new file already leaves the camera, date and GPS details out.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com if a detail was left in a clean copy, and describe the photo and the app that made it (no personal data, and please don't attach the photo).

All of these place a picture of your signature on the page. If the person who asked for the signature needs a certificate-based digital signature, you also need a digital ID, and LibreOffice can apply one for free.In your browser, with nothing uploadedSign PDF works on any computer or phone with a modern browser, and the PDF never leaves your device:Open Sign PDF and choose your PDF, or drop it on the page.Click Create signature, then draw it with a mouse, finger or pen, type your name in one of three signature styles, or upload a photo of your signature (a white background can be made see-through).Drag the signature where it belongs and drag its corner to make it bigger or smaller.To sign every page, select the signature and copy it to all pages or to the pages you type, such as 1-3, 5.Click Save a copy, check the preview and download the signed PDF. Your signature is kept only while the page is open.On a Mac: PreviewPreview, the PDF app that comes with every Mac, signs PDFs without any download. Open the PDF in Preview, show the Markup toolbar and click the Sign button. Create a signature with the trackpad, with the Mac's camera (sign on white paper and hold it up), or with an iPhone or iPad, then click the signature to place it and drag it into position. Saved signatures are available on your other Macs that use iCloud Drive. Apple describes the steps in its Preview guide.On an iPhone or iPad: MarkupOpen the PDF in the Files app, tap the Markup button (a pen tip in a circle), tap the plus button and choose Add Signature. Draw your signature with your finger, tap Done, then drag and resize it on the page. If an app does not show Markup, save the PDF to Files first and open it there. Saved signatures can be reused on the next document.On Windows: Microsoft EdgeMicrosoft Edge, the browser that comes with Windows, opens PDFs and has a Draw tool. Open the PDF in Edge, choose Draw, write your signature with a mouse, pen or finger, then save the PDF. It is quick, but the signature is drawn freehand each time; Sign PDF in the browser lets you type or upload one instead and copy it to every page.A picture of a signature is not a digital signatureEvery method above adds a visual signature: a picture of your handwriting placed on the page, like signing a printout. It does not prove who signed, and someone with a PDF editor could copy it.A certificate-based digital signature is different. It uses a digital ID issued to you (by an employer, a bank, a government service or a certificate authority) and seals the file, so any later change shows. Some contracts, government forms and regulated processes require this kind.If you have a digital ID, LibreOffice can sign an existing PDF with it for free: open LibreOffice, choose File, Digital Signatures, Sign Existing PDF, and follow the steps. Whether a visual signature is enough depends on who asked for it; when in doubt, ask them or your legal team.Before you send itA few checks save a second round:Open the signed PDF again and look at every signed page; in OpenAnyDoc the preview shows the first pages before you download.If the PDF is a form, fill in its fields first with Fill PDF form, and tick Flatten on save so the answers cannot be changed.If you need to send several signed documents as one file, put them together with Merge PDF.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe what you need (no personal data).

title: Spreadsheet to AI Chat: Paste a Table It Can Actually Read
desc: How to give ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini a spreadsheet it can read: Markdown table or CSV, one sheet at a time, size in tokens, formulas, and hiding personal data.
h1s: How do I give an AI chat a spreadsheet it can read?
headings: How do I give an AI chat a spreadsheet it can read?
Why not paste the cells or attach the workbook?
text: HomeGuidesSpreadsheet to AI chatHow do I give an AI chat a spreadsheet it can read?Turn one sheet into a Markdown table, check its size in tokens and hide personal data before you paste it into a chat.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerTurn the sheet you need into a Markdown table with Excel to Markdown, check how many tokens it takes, and paste it into the chat with a sentence saying what the columns mean. A Markdown table keeps every value under its column name, so ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini can read it row by row. Hide names, emails and other personal data first; the chat keeps whatever you paste.Why not paste the cells or attach the workbook?Copying cells out of Excel gives tab-separated text. That works for a small range, but in a chat box the tabs are invisible and a reader, human or AI, has to count them to know which value belongs to which column.Attaching the .xlsx file sends the whole workbook: every sheet, hidden ones included, plus anything else stored in it. Often you only want one table read. Converting first means you choose exactly what leaves your device, and you can see it before you send it.Markdown table or CSV?Both work. The difference is readability against size. In our test, a synthetic table of 100 orders with 5 columns took 1,759 tokens as a Markdown table and 1,367 tokens as CSV, so the Markdown version was about 29% larger. The extra tokens are the pipes and the separator line.Choose a Markdown table when the table is small or medium, when cells contain commas, or when you want the chat to show the same table back to you.Choose CSV when the table is large and every token counts. Excel to CSV gives you the file; open it in any text editor and paste its text.For lists of records in JSON, the TOON format can be shorter still; see what TOON is and when it saves tokens.One sheet at a timeExcel to Markdown converts the sheet you pick from its sheet list, one table per conversion. That is deliberate: two sheets with different columns pasted as one block confuse the reader about where one table ends. If the chat needs two sheets, paste them as two tables, each under a line such as "Sheet: Budget 2026".To see what the whole workbook costs before you decide, drop it on the token counter: it counts every sheet, each written as a Markdown table under its sheet name.Formulas or shown values?The table holds each cell as Excel shows it. A formula appears as its result, and dates, percentages and prices keep their format, so 0.15 formatted as a percentage arrives as 15%. That is usually what you want the chat to reason about.The formulas themselves are not in the table. If you want the chat to check or explain a formula, copy it from the formula bar and paste it as a separate line, with the cell it lives in. Merged cells give their value to the first cell of the range, and colours, fonts and comments are not kept, so if a colour carries meaning, add a column that says it in words.How big is too big?Chats measure what you paste in tokens, and the limit depends on the model and your plan. Long pastes can be refused, cut, or answered less carefully toward the end. Count first: the token counter shows the tokens, words and characters of a file or pasted text in your browser. Its count follows one common tokenizer, so for other models the number is an estimate.If the number is high, make the table smaller before you paste it:Delete the columns the question does not need. IDs, internal codes and long notes are often the largest.Keep only the rows the question is about, or send a summary instead, made with Pivot table.Split a long table into parts with Split CSV and send them one message at a time.Hide personal data firstOnce pasted, the data is on the chat service's servers under its rules, not yours. If the sheet holds customer names, emails, phone numbers or ID numbers, run it through Mask data before you convert it. It finds those columns, replaces each value with a token such as EMAIL-000001, and gives the same value the same token everywhere, so the chat can still count, group and compare rows. Keep the private key if you want to put the real values back later. The guide to anonymizing a file before sharing explains the choices.Step by stepThe whole routine takes a minute, and the workbook is read by your browser at every step:Mask the workbook if it holds personal data, and save the masked copy.Open Excel to Markdown, choose the workbook and pick the sheet.Copy the table, paste it into the token counter if you are unsure of its size, and trim it if needed.In the chat, write one sentence about the table (what a row is, what each unclear column means), then paste the table and ask your question.Other filesThe same idea works for documents: a PDF with tables can go through PDF to Markdown, and the guides on Word documents and PowerPoint decks cover their own catches. For a CSV file, CSV to Markdown does the same job as the Excel tool.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe the sheet and what the chat got wrong (no personal data).

title: Stirling-PDF Alternative That Runs in Your Browser
desc: Stirling-PDF vs a browser-only PDF toolkit: where files are processed, what you must host, plans and limits, from its own pages, and where Stirling does more.
h1s: A Stirling-PDF alternative that needs no server
headings: A Stirling-PDF alternative that needs no server
text: HomeGuidesStirling-PDF alternativeA Stirling-PDF alternative that needs no serverHow Stirling-PDF handles your files, where it does more, and PDF tools that keep every file on the employee's own device.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026 · Updated November 23, 2026The short answerStirling-PDF is a PDF toolkit you run on your own server, so files go from your staff's browsers to a machine you control and are processed there. OpenAnyDoc does the work inside each person's browser instead, so there is no server to run and the file never leaves the device. Stirling-PDF has far more operations, an API and automation; OpenAnyDoc is the lighter choice when everyday PDF tasks are what people need.How Stirling-PDF works (checked 20 November 2026)What Stirling-PDF says on its own pages; follow the links for the current wording:Self-hosted server: the GitHub README starts it with one Docker command and describes it as something you can "deploy on your own servers with a private API". The Docker guide lists three images, from a core-only one (about 2 GB of memory suggested) to a full one with a bundled AI engine (6 GB suggested).Where files are processed: its page on where tools run says that in a self-hosted setup "every tool runs on your server, even ones your computer could run". The desktop app also has a local-only mode in which nothing is uploaded, and an administrator can turn on local processing.Features: the README lists "50+ PDF tools", including edit, merge, split, sign, redact, convert, OCR and compress, plus no-code pipelines and REST APIs for nearly all tools.Licence: the README calls Stirling-PDF "open-core". Its LICENSE file is MIT for most of the code, with several directories under their own separate licences.Plans: its plans page says a self-hosted server runs on the Free plan (5 users, 1,000 monthly processing units) until you add Team or Enterprise. The pricing page lists Team at $99 a month with 100 users; Enterprise is custom and adds SAML single sign-on, audit logging and air-gapped deployment.Stirling Cloud: its files and privacy page says compress, OCR, convert and watermark files are sent to Stirling's servers, processed and returned.Where Stirling-PDF does moreTo be fair about the choice, Stirling-PDF covers ground that OpenAnyDoc does not:Many more operations than OpenAnyDoc has.Pipelines that chain several steps and run on many files without anyone clicking through them.A REST API, so other systems in your company can send PDFs to it.Accounts, single sign-on and, on the paid plans, audit logging, which matter when you must show who did what.Server-side work that does not depend on the speed or memory of each employee's computer.What OpenAnyDoc does differentlyOpenAnyDoc has more than 30 PDF tools, and every one runs in the browser of the person using it. The file is read, changed and saved on that device. The page's security policy only lets it contact its own site, so a document cannot be sent anywhere else; anyone can confirm this in the browser's network panel, as the guide to check this yourself explains.Keeping files in-house therefore does not need a processing server. Because the site is a folder of static files, an organisation can host its own copy on an internal network: build it and serve the folder from any web server. There is no database, no user accounts, no Docker image to keep up to date and no processing limit, and the files employees open still never leave their devices. The source code is public on GitHub. Once a page has loaded, the tools also work offline.Side by sideThe main differences, in short:Where files are processed: Stirling-PDF self-hosted, on your server; OpenAnyDoc, in each user's browser.What you run: Stirling-PDF, a Docker container or desktop app with 2 to 6 GB of memory suggested; OpenAnyDoc, nothing, or static files on any web server.Users and limits: Stirling-PDF Free, 5 users and 1,000 processing units a month; OpenAnyDoc, no accounts and no limits.Operations: Stirling-PDF, 50+ tools with pipelines and an API; OpenAnyDoc, more than 30 PDF tools with no API.Compression: both; OpenAnyDoc re-saves pictures at three quality levels in the browser and does not lower their resolution.Large batches: Stirling-PDF, handled by the server; OpenAnyDoc, limited by each device's memory.The PDF tools OpenAnyDoc coversEach of these works on the user's own device:Merge, split, remove or extract pages, organize, rotate and crop.Edit, sign and fill in PDF forms; add page numbers, a watermark, or a header and footer; redact and compare.OCR PDF makes a scanned PDF searchable in English or Arabic; the reader is loaded from the site itself on first use.Protect PDF locks a file with a password and AES-256 encryption; Unlock PDF removes a password you know.Convert Word and Excel to PDF, and PDF to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, JPG, text or Markdown.Who should stay with Stirling-PDFKeep Stirling-PDF, or choose it, if you need to run the same steps on thousands of files, call PDF tools from other software through an API, or log who processed which document. Those are server jobs, and a browser tool is not built for them. Many teams can use both: Stirling-PDF for automation, OpenAnyDoc for everyday tasks that should never reach a server.Which to chooseA simple rule of thumb:Staff need everyday PDF tasks and you do not want to run a server: OpenAnyDoc, hosted by us or on your own network.You need automation, an API or audit logs: Stirling-PDF.Your rules say documents may not leave the employee's device at all: a tool that processes them locally.You are unsure what your rules allow: ask your IT or compliance team first. More options are in PDF tools that do not upload your file.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe what you need, for example hosting a copy on your network (no personal data).

Whole URL: : / ? & = # and the other address characters kept, the same as encodeURI.
Spaces: encoded as %20.
Text: read as UTF-8, so Arabic letters and emoji become their %XX bytes and decode back exactly.
Errors: invalid percent sequences, such as %G1 or a lone %, are reported.

mainEntity.name: Is my text uploaded?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Encoding and decoding run in your browser, on your device, and your text stays in this tab. It is never sent anywhere or saved on the site, and there are no share links or history.

mainEntity.name: Which mode should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Part of a URL when you are building one value, such as a search term or a redirect address that goes after ?q=. Use Whole URL when you have a complete link with spaces or Arabic letters in it and want it to stay a working address.

mainEntity.name: Why is a space %20 and not +?

acceptedAnswer.text: %20 is how a space is written in any part of a URL. The + form only applies to data sent by HTML forms, and this tool does not offer it.

mainEntity.name: What does "invalid percent sequence" mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: A % must be followed by two hexadecimal digits, and together they must form valid UTF-8. Something like %G1, a % at the end, or half of an Arabic letter's bytes can't be decoded, so the page reports it.

mainEntity.name: Does it work with Arabic and other languages?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Text is turned into UTF-8 bytes, and each byte is written as %XX. Decoding reads them back into the same letters.

mainEntity.name: Is it free, and does it work offline?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes to both. There is no account or limit, and once the page has loaded it keeps working without an internet connection.

mainEntity.name: How do I decode a URL?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decode a URL by turning each %XX sequence back into the character it stands for, so %20 becomes a space and %D8%A7 becomes the Arabic letter ا. In OpenAnyDoc, paste the link and press Decode; the text stays in your browser and is never sent anywhere.

mainEntity.name: Will the JPG be bigger?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually a little, because WebP compresses better. Choose a quality of about 80 to keep it close.

mainEntity.name: Is it really free?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. There is no account, no watermark and no limit on how often you use it.

mainEntity.name: What is a WebP file?

acceptedAnswer.text: A WebP file is a picture format made for the web: it is smaller than JPG or PNG at the same look and can keep transparency. Every modern browser opens it, but some photo apps, printers and upload forms do not, which is when converting to JPG helps.

title: What Is TOON Format? JSON vs TOON and When It Saves Tokens
desc: TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) explained: what it looks like next to JSON, how to read it, and measured token counts for uniform lists and nested data.
h1s: What is the TOON format, and when does it save tokens?
headings: What is the TOON format, and when does it save tokens?
What it looks like next to JSON
When it saves tokens, in our test
text: HomeGuidesWhat is TOON?What is the TOON format, and when does it save tokens?TOON writes the same data as JSON in fewer tokens, but only for some shapes of data. Here is what it looks like and what our own counts showed.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerTOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) is an open text format for the same data as JSON, made to use fewer tokens when you paste data into an AI chat. It writes a list of objects with the same keys as one header line of field names and then one row of values per item, and nested objects with indentation instead of braces. It saves a lot on long, uniform lists and little or nothing on deeply nested or irregular data, especially compared with minified JSON.What it looks like next to JSONTake three synthetic orders. Formatted JSON repeats every key for every order and spends a line on each brace, 137 tokens in our test. The same data in TOON is four lines and 60 tokens:orders[3]{id,product,quantity,price,status}: 1001,Notebook,1,0.5,paid 1002,Pen,8,13.5,shipped 1003,Stapler,3,26.5,pendingHow to read itThe first line says: a list called orders, with 3 items, and these five fields. Each indented line is one item, with its values in the order of the fields. The item count and the field names act as a check, so a reader can tell when a row is missing or has a value too many.Data that is not a uniform list looks like indented key: value lines, much like YAML. Text is quoted only when it has to be, for example a version written as "1.2" keeps its quotes so it stays text and is not read as a number. A list of mixed items is written with a dash before each item.When it saves tokens, in our testWe converted three synthetic samples with the same converter and token count the JSON to TOON page uses. The comparison depends on the JSON you start from, so each sample was counted as formatted JSON (indented with 2 spaces) and as minified JSON (one line):100 orders with the same 5 keys: 4,291 tokens formatted, 2,387 minified, 1,571 as TOON. TOON was 63% smaller than formatted JSON and 34% smaller than minified JSON.A nested settings object, five levels deep: 236 formatted, 122 minified, 153 as TOON. Smaller than formatted JSON, but 25% larger than minified JSON.30 events of three different shapes: 1,239 formatted, 644 minified, 818 as TOON. Again smaller than formatted JSON and 27% larger than minified.Why the shape mattersTOON saves tokens by writing each key once for a whole list. When items share their keys, that removes most of the repetition. When there is no list to share keys across, as in a settings object or a mix of different records, there is nothing to remove, and the indentation TOON uses instead of braces costs about as much as the braces it replaces. Minified JSON has no indentation at all, which is why it beat TOON on those two samples.One more comparison from the same test: the 100 orders as a plain CSV table took 1,367 tokens, fewer than TOON. For a flat table with no nesting, CSV or a Markdown table is just as good a choice; the guide on giving an AI chat a spreadsheet compares those two.Use TOON whenA quick rule from the numbers above:Use it for long lists of records with the same keys, such as API responses, exports and logs, especially when they have a few nested fields that CSV cannot hold.Skip it for configuration files, deeply nested documents and lists whose items all differ; minify the JSON instead with Minify JSON.Skip it for small data. Saving 50 tokens is not worth explaining a new format to the chat.Measure your own dataPaste the JSON into JSON to TOON and it shows the token count before and after and the saving in percent. The "before" count is the JSON as you pasted it, so formatted JSON shows a bigger saving than the same data minified. For a fair test, minify it first, then convert. The counts follow one common tokenizer, so for other models they are estimates; the token counter uses the same count.The conversion runs in your browser and nothing is sent to a server or to any AI service. If the data holds names, emails or ID numbers, hide them first with Mask data.Will a chat understand it?TOON is new, and not every tool knows it by name. When you paste it into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, say in one sentence that the data is in TOON format and that the first line lists the fields. The header line makes the rows easy to follow even for a reader who has never seen the format.TOON is also two-way: when a chat answers in TOON, or you want your data back, choose TOON to JSON on the JSON to TOON page to turn it back into ordinary JSON.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe the shape of your data and the counts you saw (no personal data).

title: Word Document to AI Chat Without Losing Headings or Lists
desc: Give a Word .docx file to ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini with its headings, lists and links kept as Markdown, plus a step for tables. In your browser, no upload.
h1s: How to give a Word document to an AI chat and keep its structure
headings: How to give a Word document to an AI chat and keep its structure
What gets lost when you copy from Word
Get the headings right in Word first
text: HomeGuidesWord document to AI chatHow to give a Word document to an AI chat and keep its structureWhy pasted Word text loses its outline, what Markdown keeps, how to handle tables, and what to check before you paste.By OpenAnyDoc · Published November 20, 2026The short answerConvert the .docx file to Markdown and paste that. Markdown marks Word's headings with #, ## and ###, keeps bulleted and numbered lists as lists and keeps links with their address, so ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini can follow the outline of the document. OpenAnyDoc's Word to Markdown does it in your browser without uploading the file. Tables become Markdown tables too.What gets lost when you copy from WordWord shows structure with styles: a heading is a paragraph with the Heading 1 style, a list is a paragraph with numbering switched on. Many chat boxes keep only the plain text of what you paste, so the styles are gone and a section title looks like any other line. On a long document the AI then has to guess where one part ends and the next begins.Attaching the .docx instead sends the whole file to the AI service, including comments, tracked changes or hidden text you may have forgotten about, and you cannot see which parts it actually read.What Markdown keepsMarkdown carries the structure as ordinary characters, so it survives any paste:Headings: Word's heading styles become #, ## and ###.Bold and italic text keep their marks.Bulleted and numbered lists stay lists, with sub-points indented under their parent.Links keep their address.Pictures, charts and shapes are left out; only the text is converted.How to do itWord to Markdown runs on your device, and nothing is sent to a server or to an AI service:Open Word to Markdown and choose a .docx, .dotx or .docm file, or drop it on the page.The Markdown appears in a text box, with its token count.Read it through, then click Copy and paste it into the chat, or download the .md file.Get the headings right in Word firstHeadings are found from Word's heading styles, not from how text looks. A line you made bold and large by hand stays an ordinary paragraph. Before converting, click into each section title and choose Heading 1, Heading 2 or Heading 3 from the Styles list; the Navigation pane in Word shows which titles it already sees as headings.Old .doc files and OpenDocument .odt files are not read here. Open them in Word or LibreOffice and save them as .docx first. If you only want to read an .odt file, the Word viewer opens it.TablesWord to Markdown turns each table into a Markdown table, with the table's first row as the header row, so an AI chat reads the rows and columns instead of a run of loose cells. Markdown has no merged cells, so a table with merged cells or a table inside a table comes out flattened. When such a table matters, copy it from Word into a spreadsheet such as Excel or LibreOffice Calc, fix the layout there and save it as .xlsx; Excel to Markdown then turns that sheet into a clean Markdown table you can paste under the rest of the document. The same idea works for a table inside a PDF; see giving an AI chat a PDF without losing the tables.Before you pasteTwo checks are worth the minute they take:Personal data: contracts, reports and letters often hold names, email addresses, phone numbers or ID numbers. Mask data replaces them on your device; it reads plain text files, so rename the downloaded .md file to .txt and open it there.Length: the token count under the result shows how much of the chat the document will fill. Token counter explains the number, and other models count a little differently.Ask by sectionOnce the Markdown is in the chat, you can point at parts of the document by their headings: rewrite the section called Payment terms in plain language, list every deadline under Delivery, or check that the summary matches the sections after it. Requests like these work only when the headings came through, which is the main reason to convert rather than paste.Slides and PDFsA presentation needs a different shape, one section per slide with its speaker notes; see giving a PowerPoint deck to an AI chat. For a PDF, use PDF to Markdown.Questions?Write to support@openanydoc.com and describe the document (no personal data).

mainEntity.name: Is OpenAnyDoc really free?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Opening, viewing, editing and downloading your files is free, with no account and no sign-up.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to open my files online? Are they uploaded?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your files are not uploaded. Your browser reads the file and shows it on your screen, so it never leaves your device and there is nothing for us to store, see or lose.

mainEntity.name: Which file types can I open?

acceptedAnswer.text: CSV and tab-separated tables (.csv, .tsv, .tab), plain text (.txt), JSON (.json), Excel (.xlsx, .xls, .xlsm, .ods) Word documents (.docx, .dotx, .docm, .odt), PowerPoint presentations (.pptx, .ppsx, .potx, .pptm, in beta) and PDF files (.pdf) to view. Old .doc and .ppt files are not supported.

mainEntity.name: Can I edit my file and save the changes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for CSV, TXT, JSON and Excel files: make your changes, with undo and redo, and download a copy in the same format. The file on your device is never changed and edits are not kept anywhere else, so download before you leave. Excel files keep formulas, number formats and merged cells; charts, images and macros are not kept.

mainEntity.name: How big can a file be?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no fixed limit for CSV, TXT and Excel; it depends on your browser's memory. Files over 50 MB show a warning, and OpenAnyDoc still tries to open them. JSON files are the exception: they open up to 10 MB. A 120,000-row CSV file opens in under a second, and a 46 MB text file has been tested.

mainEntity.name: Does it handle Arabic and other Unicode text?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. UTF-8 (with or without a BOM) and UTF-16 files are read directly, and a file that is not valid UTF-8 is read as Windows-1256. Arabic cells display right-to-left.

mainEntity.name: Does it work on my phone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Every viewer works in a phone browser: the CSV, JSON and TXT pages have their own phone layouts, and the Excel page adapts to a small screen. Big sheets are easier on a larger screen.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to install anything or create an account?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. OpenAnyDoc runs in your browser, with no install and no account.
